analysis.one_liner: Requires presidents to publicly release their recent and in-office tax returns.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in February 2019, received no hearings or votes, and died when the 116th Congress ended without any return disclosure requirement becoming law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any president to hand tax returns — including the three years before taking office and every return filed while in office — to the Office of Government Ethics, which would post them online within seven business days, with only Social Security numbers, account numbers, and dependents' names redacted. If a president refused, the Treasury Secretary would be directed to release the returns anyway, and knowingly hiding or falsifying them would carry civil and criminal penalties. It was referred to two House committees, neither acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would gain the same view of a president's income, tax rate, debts, and business entanglements that presidents have long asked of Cabinet nominees, making it harder to hide policies that personally enrich the officeholder. Honest candidates who disclose voluntarily would also benefit from a level playing field.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting to see a president's finances

how_it_helps.text: Voters could see the president's income, tax rates, business holdings, and debts before and during his term, making it easier to spot policies that enrich him personally.
It would apply to every future president, not just one: any individual assuming the office after 2016 would have to disclose three years of prior returns plus all returns filed while in office.

analysis.who_pays: Presidents and their families, who would lose the ability to keep their finances and business dealings private while in office, and would face fines or jail time for hiding or falsifying returns.

drawbacks.text: The bill requires disclosure even of returns under audit; a president could argue compelled public disclosure of unaudited, complex returns invites misleading attacks or harassment unrelated to ethics enforcement.

The penalty for non-compliance — a fine of up to $50,000 and up to six months' imprisonment — is modest for a wealthy officeholder, and enforcement depends on an Attorney General willing to sue a sitting or former president.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: every modern major-party nominee until 2016 had voluntarily released returns, and a statutory requirement restores that norm without relying on any one president's goodwill. The costs are small — audits could reveal sensitive financial details, and a sitting president might view compelled disclosure as harassing — but the bill's near-certain futility (no hearing, no vote, no Senate companion moving) meant it mostly functioned as a statement about the sitting president's refusal to disclose, not as an achievable reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees in February 2019, neither committee ever took it up, and it sat there until the Congress expired with no vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: H.R. 950 was introduced on February 4, 2019 and referred to the House Oversight and Reform Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred.

As written, the bill would have required the president to submit tax returns to the Office of Government Ethics, which would post them online within seven business days, with only Social Security numbers, tax ID numbers, account numbers, and dependents' names redacted.

If the president refused to submit the returns, the bill directed the Treasury Secretary to disclose them to OGE directly, and it created civil and criminal penalties — up to $50,000 and six months in prison — for knowingly falsifying or failing to disclose.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Any president who wants to keep tax returns and business finances secret — including the sitting president, whose returns stayed private — is better off; the public learned nothing new from congressional action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidents who prefer keeping tax returns secret

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: President Donald Trump
against.what_they_did: Refused throughout the 116th Congress to release his tax returns, breaking a four-decade practice by major-party nominees, which made any disclosure mandate politically contested and gave committee chairmen little incentive to advance it.

against.name: House Republican caucus
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors and supported the status quo of no presidential return disclosure; no Republican backed the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Democratic-controlled House either, so it lacked majority-committee support rather than failing on a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Presidents and their private business interests
industries.note: The bill would force any sitting president to publicly disclose the tax returns that reveal the size and sources of his or her private fortune, closing the loophole that let the sitting president keep his finances secret. Its death preserved that privacy.
